rejected.title: Selective breeding
card: In selective breeding, humans choose which organisms breed, based on traits they want. Examples are milk yield in cows and sweetness in fruit.
Only the chosen individuals pass on their alleles. Breeding does not create new alleles, but over many generations the alleles for wanted traits become more common, so allele frequencies change.
Humans, not the environment, decide which individuals reproduce most. This is the difference from natural selection.
Breeders often use a small number of parents, so many alleles are lost and genetic diversity falls. If conditions change, such as a new disease, the population may lack alleles that help it survive.
rejected.remember: Selective breeding: humans pick the parents, wanted alleles rise, and diversity falls.

a.q: A farmer breeds only the sheep with the softest wool for many generations. What happens to the sheep population?
opts: Alleles for soft wool become more common
Alleles for soft wool become less common
Allele frequencies stay the same
New alleles for soft wool appear because it is needed
a.why: Only the softest-wool sheep pass on their alleles, so alleles linked to soft wool become more common. It is wrong to say the need for soft wool creates new alleles, because breeding changes the frequency of alleles that already exist.
a.clue: Which sheep get to pass on their alleles?

b.q: Mia breeds show dogs using only a few champion males, and many alleles have been lost. Why is the breed more at risk if a new disease appears?
opts: Fewer different alleles, so resistant ones may be missing
Wanted alleles become rarer, so the dogs lose variation
New alleles appear when needed, but too slowly to help
The environment, not the breeder, now picks the parents
b.why: Using few parents loses alleles, so there is less variation. If a disease appears, the breed may have no alleles that help dogs resist it. Selective breeding makes wanted alleles more common, not rarer, and it does not create new alleles when they are needed.
b.clue: What does a population need to already have when conditions change?

b.q: Mia breeds show dogs from just a few champion males, and the breed now has far fewer different alleles. Why is this a risk for the breed?
opts: Low diversity means fewer alleles to cope with a new disease
Low diversity means mutations can no longer occur
Low diversity means the dogs can no longer reproduce
Low diversity means nature now chooses which dogs breed
b.why: Using few parents loses alleles, so the population has less variation. If a new disease appears, there may be no resistant alleles. Humans still choose the parents, so the environment is not the one choosing.

b.q: Mia breeds show dogs using only a few champion males for many generations. A new disease then spreads through the breed. Why is the breed at greater risk than a mixed-breed dog population?
opts: It has lower diversity, so protective alleles may be absent
It has higher diversity, so harmful alleles may be common
It has lower diversity, so new alleles may arise too often
It has higher diversity, so natural selection may be blocked
b.why: Using few parents lowers genetic diversity, so the breed may lack alleles that help dogs resist the disease. The mixed population has more variation to draw on. Selective breeding does not raise diversity, and it does not create new alleles to meet a need.
